questions.prompt: Which statement about `ThreadPool` threads matches the lesson's advice?
options: They are foreground threads, so it is fine to block them for long periods
They are created fresh for each work item and discarded afterwards
They are background threads that get reused, so you shouldn't block them for long
They can only run I/O work, never CPU-bound code
questions.explanation: ThreadPool threads are background threads and reused; for long-blocking work use async I/O or dedicated threads instead of tying up a pool thread.

questions.prompt: You queue work with `ThreadPool.QueueUserWorkItem` and now need the value it computes. What does the lesson suggest?
options: Use `Task.Run`, because `QueueUserWorkItem` is fire-and-forget with no return value
Read the value from the `state` argument after the call returns
Call `ThreadPool.GetAvailableThreads` to collect the result
Pass `executeOnlyOnce: true` so the callback returns its value
questions.explanation: `QueueUserWorkItem` is fire-and-forget and has no return value; use `Task.Run` if you need a result.

options: `Sum = 0`, because `Main` doesn't wait for the task
The task's type name, because `t` is a `Task<int>`
questions.explanation: `await t` asynchronously waits for the pool work to finish and unwraps the `int` it returned, so it prints the sum of 1 to 1000, which is 500500.

questions.prompt: A `Task<int>` faults with an `InvalidOperationException`. What happens when you read `t.Result`?
options: It returns `0`, the default for `int`
It throws the `InvalidOperationException` directly, just like `await`
It returns immediately without blocking and sets `t.Status` to `Canceled`
It throws an `AggregateException` that wraps the `InvalidOperationException`
questions.explanation: `.Result` blocks until the task finishes and, if it faulted, throws an `AggregateException` wrapping the original exception; `await` unwraps exceptions automatically.

questions.prompt: You have heavy blocking work that will run for a long time. Why might you use `Task.Factory.StartNew` instead of `Task.Run`?
options: `StartNew` is the newer API and always faster
`StartNew` lets you pass `TaskCreationOptions.LongRunning`, hinting the scheduler to use a dedicated thread
`StartNew` runs the work on the calling thread, avoiding the pool
`Task.Run` cannot run work that calls `Thread.Sleep`
questions.explanation: `Task.Factory.StartNew` is the older API; use it when you need `TaskCreationOptions` such as `LongRunning`, which hints that a dedicated thread may be created. Otherwise prefer `Task.Run`.

questions.prompt: Which option waits for several tasks without blocking the current thread?
options: `Task.WaitAll(t1, t2)`
`t1.Wait(); t2.Wait();`
`await Task.WhenAll(t1, t2)`
Reading `t1.Result` and `t2.Result`
questions.explanation: `Task.Wait()` and `Task.WaitAll(...)` are blocking waits, while `Task.WhenAll(...)` is non-blocking composition that returns a `Task` you can await.
